screens.title: Interacting with the World State
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the World State — the ledger’s current, queryable key-value database — and the practical techniques you will use from chaincode to read and update it. You’ll learn why the blockchain is best thought of as an immutable transaction journal while the World State is the up-to-date balance sheet, and why that separation makes querying efficient. We’ll cover the core calls you use every day: PutState, GetState, and DelState, and show how values must be marshaled as JSON bytes before storage. You will also see two approaches for richer queries: composite keys that let you index multi-attribute data when LevelDB is in use, and CouchDB rich queries that allow JSON selectors and complex filters when CouchDB is configured. Concrete code snippets will walk through the GetStateByRange iterator pattern and a complete GetAllAssets implementation, plus common mistakes to avoid, such as attempting rich queries against LevelDB or mis-ordering attributes in a composite key. By the end you’ll understand how to choose an approach, and how to write efficient, safe chaincode queries that scale.

screens.title: World State: current snapshot vs transaction log
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear mental model: the blockchain is the immutable transaction journal and the World State is the current snapshot of assets. The blockchain stores every transaction in append-only blocks; it records how the state changed over time. The World State, by contrast, contains the latest key-value records for each asset so that reads return current values without scanning history. This separation matters because chaincode typically needs the latest view of an asset, not the full history, and using the World State yields far faster lookup. A concrete example: if you want the current owner of asset1, a GetState on the World State returns it directly; scanning the blockchain would require reading many transactions and reconstructing the final value. A common misconception is that the World State stores history — it does not. If you need historical versions, query the blockchain's transaction log rather than relying on World State. Key takeaway: design chaincode to use the World State for live reads and use the blockchain only when you require an auditable history. World State: current snapshot vs transaction log means use the world state for current-value queries, and the blockchain for audit and history.. In practical terms, understand the different roles of blockchain and world state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Snapshot vs Journal
keyIdea.text: Use the World State for current-value queries, and the blockchain for audit and history.

content.html:
Core Concept

World State vs Blockchain

The World State is a key-value database holding the latest values; the blockchain is the immutable ledger of transactions that produced those values.

Concrete example
GetState("asset1") returns the current owner without replaying prior transactions.
Misconception check
The World State is not an audit trail; do not store historical versions there.
Key Takeaway

Prefer World State for live reads; query blockchain for history or forensic analysis.

Analogy: journal vs balance sheet
Blockchain = transaction journal recording every change. World State = current balance sheet that summarizes outcomes.
Blockchain
  • Append-only
  • History retention
  • Audit queries
World State
  • Key-value store
  • Fast current lookups
  • Updated by transactions

screens.title: Basic state APIs: PutState, GetState, DelState
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode interacts with the World State through a small set of fundamental A P I calls. PutState creates or updates a key-value pair. GetState retrieves the byte array value for a given string key. DelState removes a key and its value. A critical implementation detail is that value parameters are byte arrays — structured data such as asset structs must be marshaled to JSON bytes before PutState and unmarshaled back into a struct after GetState. For example, when saving an Asset you would convert it to JSON bytes then call PutState with the asset ID as key. When reading, GetState returns the raw bytes which you must unmarshal. A common error is to assume values are typed fields rather than bytes; this leads to runtime unmarshaling errors. Another pitfall is overwriting keys without version checks; for concurrent updates consider reading the state and including checks or using endorsements that guard against conflicting writes. Key takeaway: treat keys as strings and values as opaque JSON byte blobs that you control through marshaling and unmarshaling. Basic state APIs: PutState, GetState, DelState means keys are strings; values are byte arrays. marshal structured data to json bytes before storage and unmarshal after retrieval.. In practical terms, storing, retrieving, and deleting asset records. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: API contract
keyIdea.text: Keys are strings; values are byte arrays. Marshal structured data to JSON bytes before storage and unmarshal after retrieval.

content.html:
Definition

PutState / GetState / DelState

PutState writes JSON-marshaled bytes using a string key. GetState returns the bytes for that key. DelState removes the entry.

Concrete example
key: "asset1" value: JSON bytes of Asset struct
Misconception check
Values are not native Go structs in storage; they are byte arrays that must be marshaled/unmarshaled.
Key Takeaway

Always marshal structs to JSON bytes before PutState and unmarshal after GetState to reconstruct the object.

Practical pattern
// Marshal before storing
assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
if err != nil { return err }
err = ctx.GetStub().PutState(asset.ID, assetJSON)

// Read and unmarshal
assetBytes, err := ctx.GetStub().GetState(assetID)
if err != nil { return nil, err }
if assetBytes == nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("asset not found") }
err = json.Unmarshal(assetBytes, &asset)
This pattern ensures values are consistently encoded and decoded across chaincode functions and peers.

screens.title: Implementing GetAllAssets with GetStateByRange
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to retrieve all assets in a chaincode namespace is to perform an open-ended range query with GetStateByRange using empty start and end keys. The call returns a StateQueryIteratorInterface which you must iterate through and close when finished. The provided GetAllAssets example demonstrates the full pattern: obtain the iterator, defer Close to ensure resources are released even on error, loop while HasNext is true, call Next to get each record, unmarshal the returned bytes into an Asset struct, and append it to a result slice. This approach is straightforward for small ledgers or testing, but it’s potentially expensive for large ledgers because it reads every key. A common misuse is forgetting to defer Close, which can leak resources, or assuming Next will never return an error. In production, prefer targeted queries—composite keys or CouchDB selectors—over open-ended scans. Practice: walk through the provided Go function, run it on a test ledger, and observe the iterator lifecycle. The practice shows you both the mechanism and the operational risk of full scans. Implementing GetAllAssets with GetStateByRange means use getstatebyrange("","") for full scans, always defer resultsiterator.close(), and unmarshal each value before appending.. In practical terms, range queries and iterator pattern in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iterator pattern
keyIdea.text: Use GetStateByRange("","") for full scans, always defer resultsIterator.Close(), and unmarshal each Value before appending.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

GetAllAssets implementation

Open-ended range query and iterator handling example. Note the defer Close to avoid leaks.

// GetAllAssets returns all assets found in the world state
func (s *SmartContract) GetAllAssets(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface) ([]*Asset, error) {
	resultsIterator, err := ctx.GetStub().GetStateByRange("", "")
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	defer resultsIterator.Close() // IMPORTANT: Always close the iterator

	var assets []*Asset
	for resultsIterator.HasNext() {
		queryResponse, err := resultsIterator.Next()
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}

		var asset Asset
		err = json.Unmarshal(queryResponse.Value, &asset)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		assets = append(assets, &asset)
	}

	return assets, nil
}
Explanation
  • GetStateByRange("","") returns all keys in the chaincode namespace.
  • Always defer Close on the iterator to free resources.
  • Unmarshal each queryResponse.Value before using the asset.
Example scenario
Use this function in a test environment to export all ledger assets for verification, but avoid in large production ledgers.
Key Takeaway

Open-ended scans work but scale poorly; use targeted queries to limit results in production.

screens.title: Iterator lifecycle and resource safety
screens.narratorSegment: Iterators returned by GetStateByRange and GetQueryResult follow a simple lifecycle you must respect. After obtaining the iterator, defer its Close method immediately to ensure resources are released when the function returns, including on error paths. Then loop while HasNext returns true; each call to Next returns a result or an error. Handle Next errors explicitly and stop iteration if they occur. Failing to close iterators can exhaust database cursors or connections, which shows up as errors under load. A concrete example: when processing results from a rich query, you might defer Close immediately after checking the error from GetQueryResult, then run a for loop checking HasNext. Within the loop, call Next and unmarshal the value bytes into your struct. A common misconception is that Close only matters for long-running functions — it matters for every iterator because underlying peer resources are limited. Key takeaway: hold and use iterators carefully; always defer Close right after a successful iterator acquisition and check Next for errors. Iterator lifecycle and resource safety means defer close immediately after creating an iterator and handle next errors to prevent resource leaks and unexpected failures.. In practical terms, hasnext, next, and deferring close. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Defer Close immediately after creating an iterator and handle Next errors to prevent resource leaks and unexpected failures.

content.html:
Process Flow

Iterator lifecycle

1. Acquire
Call GetStateByRange or GetQueryResult and check for error.
2. Defer Close
Defer resultsIterator.Close() immediately after success to ensure cleanup.
3. Iterate
Loop while HasNext, call Next, handle errors and unmarshal values.
Concrete snippet
it, err := ctx.GetStub().GetQueryResult(query)
if err != nil { return nil, err }
defer it.Close()
for it.HasNext() {
	resp, err := it.Next()
	if err != nil { return nil, err }
	// unmarshal resp.Value
}
Misconception
Assuming Close is optional can lead to resource leaks under concurrency and should be avoided.
Key Takeaway

Always defer Close immediately, and always check Next for errors while iterating.

screens.title: LevelDB vs CouchDB
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric supports two World State backends with different trade-offs. LevelDB is the default key-value store optimized for fast direct key lookups. It performs well for PutState/GetState by key but does not support CouchDB-style rich JSON queries. CouchDB is document-oriented and enables rich queries with selector syntax, sorting, and pagination, because it indexes JSON documents. Choose LevelDB when your access pattern is primarily direct key lookups and you want lightweight configuration. Choose CouchDB when you need attribute-based querying, such as finding all assets owned by a user or filtering on multiple fields. A common error is attempting GetQueryResult against a LevelDB-backed network; this will fail. Another mistake is assuming CouchDB automatically indexes every field — you should understand index creation and performance tuning when your queries become complex. Key takeaway: match the database to your query needs: LevelDB for speed and simplicity, CouchDB for complex querying. LevelDB vs CouchDB means leveldb for simple, fast key lookups; couchdb when you require json-based rich queries and selectors.. In practical terms, choosing the world state store for your query needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: LevelDB for simple, fast key lookups; CouchDB when you require JSON-based rich queries and selectors.

content.html:
Comparison

LevelDB vs CouchDB

LevelDB (default)
  • Fast direct key lookups
  • No rich JSON selectors
  • Lightweight configuration
CouchDB (optional)
  • JSON documents and rich queries
  • Selector-based filtering and sorting
  • Needs indexing and additional config
When to use LevelDB
When most reads are GetState by ID or when you want the simplest deployment.
When to use CouchDB
When you need to run selectors like owner=="Tomoko" or color=="blue" and size > 5.
Key Takeaway

Select the World State backend based on the types of queries your chaincode will perform.

screens.title: Rich Queries and GetQueryResult
screens.narratorSegment: Rich queries are the CouchDB feature that lets you execute JSON selector-based searches against documents in the World State. In chaincode you call ctx. GetStub(). GetQueryResult(queryString) where queryString is a JSON object expressing the selector. For example, to find all assets owned by "Tomoko" you would use a selector with owner equal to Tomoko. For filtering by multiple attributes, include them in the selector — for example color equals blue and size greater than five uses an operator like dollar greater-than. The iterator returned by GetQueryResult follows the same lifecycle as range queries: check for error, defer Close, iterate and unmarshal each result. Important to remember: rich queries only work when CouchDB is configured as the World State. A typical mistake is crafting incorrectly escaped or malformed JSON for the queryString; always validate the JSON string before calling GetQueryResult. Also consider adding pagination or limiters to avoid returning huge result sets. Key takeaway: rich queries let you express attribute filters cleanly, but they depend on CouchDB and well-formed selector JSON. Rich Queries and GetQueryResult means getqueryresult accepts a json selector string for couchdb; validate and paginate your queries to avoid large result sets.. In practical terms, using couchdb selectors for attribute filtering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: This section collects the patterns that most often cause issues in production chaincode. First, attempting rich queries while LevelDB is configured will fail; always confirm the World State backend before calling GetQueryResult. Second, incomplete or malformed JSON selector strings lead to parse errors — construct selectors programmatically or validate them before use. Third, inconsistent attribute ordering when creating composite keys prevents partial matches; define and document attribute order in your contract. Fourth, never forget to defer Close on iterators; failing to close them can exhaust database resources. Fifth, avoid GetStateByRange with empty keys on large ledgers; it returns every asset and can cause timeouts or excessive memory use. Where possible, use pagination, limits, or narrower selectors. A final tip: duplicate indexing using composite keys requires additional PutState calls — account for this cost and the need to maintain those keys during updates and deletes. Key takeaway: validate backend, validate query syntax, keep key ordering consistent, and guard iterator lifecycles. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the World State — the ledger’s current, queryable key-value database — and the practical techniques you will use from chaincode to read and update it. You’ll learn why the blockchain is best thought of as an immutable transaction journal while the World State is the up-to-date balance sheet, and why that separation makes querying efficient. We’ll cover the core calls you use every day: PutState, GetState, and DelState, and show how values must be marshaled as JSON bytes before storage. You will also see two approaches for richer queries: composite keys that let you index multi-attribute data when LevelDB is in use, and CouchDB rich queries that allow JSON selectors and complex filters when CouchDB is configured. Concrete code snippets will walk through the GetStateByRange iterator pattern and a complete GetAllAssets implementation, plus common mistakes to avoid, such as attempting rich queries against LevelDB or mis-ordering attributes in a composite key. By the end you’ll understand how to choose an approach, and how to write efficient, safe chaincode queries that scale.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how the World State differs from the blockchain and why that matters for querying. You will know how to use PutState, GetState and DelState safely, including the requirement to marshal and unmarshal JSON when storing structured assets. You will be able to create and query composite keys to simulate attribute-based indexing when LevelDB is in use, and you will also be able to write basic CouchDB selector strings for use with GetQueryResult when the World State is CouchDB. Finally, you will understand how to use iterators safely and why deferring Close is essential to prevent resource leaks. Each objective includes concrete practice tasks so you can verify competency before moving on. Learning Objectives means master state api usage, choose appropriate query strategies, and avoid common iterator and database pitfalls.. Next you’ll practice basic state operations and JSON marshaling in code. Then you will apply that knowledge to design composite keys and run safe partial key queries. After that you will practice writing CouchDB selector queries and using GetQueryResult when CouchDB is available. Finally, you’ll tie everything together by choosing the most efficient approach for a scenario and validating your code with iterators and deferred cleanup. Each stage builds on the last so you can move from awareness to reproducible skill in writing optimized, safe chaincode queries. Start with a clear mental model: the blockchain is the immutable transaction journal and the World State is the current snapshot of assets. The blockchain stores every transaction in append-only blocks; it records how the state changed over time. The World State, by contrast, contains the latest key-value records for each asset so that reads return current values without scanning history. This separation matters because chaincode typically needs the latest view of an asset, not the full history, and using the World State yields far faster lookup. A concrete example: if you want the current owner of asset1, a GetState on the World State returns it directly; scanning the blockchain would require reading many transactions and reconstructing the final value. A common misconception is that the World State stores history — it does not. If you need historical versions, query the blockchain's transaction log rather than relying on World State. Key takeaway: design chaincode to use the World State for live reads and use the blockchain only when you require an auditable history. World State: current snapshot vs transaction log means use the world state for current-value queries, and the blockchain for audit and history.. In practical terms, understand the different roles of blockchain and world state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chaincode interacts with the World State through a small set of fundamental A P I calls. PutState creates or updates a key-value pair. GetState retrieves the byte array value for a given string key. DelState removes a key and its value. A critical implementation detail is that value parameters are byte arrays — structured data such as asset structs must be marshaled to JSON bytes before PutState and unmarshaled back into a struct after GetState. For example, when saving an Asset you would convert it to JSON bytes then call PutState with the asset ID as key. When reading, GetState returns the raw bytes which you must unmarshal. A common error is to assume values are typed fields rather than bytes; this leads to runtime unmarshaling errors. Another pitfall is overwriting keys without version checks; for concurrent updates consider reading the state and including checks or using endorsements that guard against conflicting writes. Key takeaway: treat keys as strings and values as opaque JSON byte blobs that you control through marshaling and unmarshaling. Basic state APIs: PutState, GetState, DelState means keys are strings; values are byte arrays. marshal structured data to json bytes before storage and unmarshal after retrieval.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A practical way to retrieve all assets in a chaincode namespace is to perform an open-ended range query with GetStateByRange using empty start and end keys. The call returns a StateQueryIteratorInterface which you must iterate through and close when finished. The provided GetAllAssets example demonstrates the full pattern: obtain the iterator, defer Close to ensure resources are released even on error, loop while HasNext is true, call Next to get each record, unmarshal the returned bytes into an Asset struct, and append it to a result slice. This approach is straightforward for small ledgers or testing, but it’s potentially expensive for large ledgers because it reads every key. A common misuse is forgetting to defer Close, which can leak resources, or assuming Next will never return an error. In production, prefer targeted queries—composite keys or CouchDB selectors—over open-ended scans. Practice: walk through the provided Go function, run it on a test ledger, and observe the iterator lifecycle. The practice shows you both the mechanism and the operational risk of full scans. Implementing GetAllAssets with GetStateByRange means use getstatebyrange("","") for full scans, always defer resultsiterator.close(), and unmarshal each value before appending.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Iterators returned by GetStateByRange and GetQueryResult follow a simple lifecycle you must respect. After obtaining the iterator, defer its Close method immediately to ensure resources are released when the function returns, including on error paths. Then loop while HasNext returns true; each call to Next returns a result or an error. Handle Next errors explicitly and stop iteration if they occur. Failing to close iterators can exhaust database cursors or connections, which shows up as errors under load. A concrete example: when processing results from a rich query, you might defer Close immediately after checking the error from GetQueryResult, then run a for loop checking HasNext. Within the loop, call Next and unmarshal the value bytes into your struct. A common misconception is that Close only matters for long-running functions — it matters for every iterator because underlying peer resources are limited. Key takeaway: hold and use iterators carefully; always defer Close right after a successful iterator acquisition and check Next for errors. Iterator lifecycle and resource safety means defer close immediately after creating an iterator and handle next errors to prevent resource leaks and unexpected failures.. In practical terms, hasnext, next, and deferring close. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fabric supports two World State backends with different trade-offs. LevelDB is the default key-value store optimized for fast direct key lookups. It performs well for PutState/GetState by key but does not support CouchDB-style rich JSON queries. CouchDB is document-oriented and enables rich queries with selector syntax, sorting, and pagination, because it indexes JSON documents. Choose LevelDB when your access pattern is primarily direct key lookups and you want lightweight configuration. Choose CouchDB when you need attribute-based querying, such as finding all assets owned by a user or filtering on multiple fields. A common error is attempting GetQueryResult against a LevelDB-backed network; this will fail. Another mistake is assuming CouchDB automatically indexes every field — you should understand index creation and performance tuning when your queries become complex. Key takeaway: match the database to your query needs: LevelDB for speed and simplicity, CouchDB for complex querying. When CouchDB is not available, composite keys provide a way to index by multiple attributes using the native LevelDB capabilities. CreateCompositeKey accepts an objectType and an ordered list of attributes; it returns a combined key such as owner~color~assetID that preserves attribute ordering for range queries. This section collects the patterns that most often cause issues in production chaincode. First, attempting rich queries while LevelDB is configured will fail; always confirm the World State backend before calling GetQueryResult. Second, incomplete or malformed JSON selector strings lead to parse errors — construct selectors programmatically or validate them before use. Third, inconsistent attribute ordering when creating composite keys prevents partial matches; define and document attribute order in your contract. Fourth, never forget to defer Close on iterators; failing to close them can exhaust database resources. Fifth, avoid GetStateByRange with empty keys on large ledgers; it returns every asset and can cause timeouts or excessive memory use. Where possible, use pagination, limits, or narrower selectors.
